slides.title: Copy Elision and RVO Overview
slides.prompt: Copy elision is an optimization technique where the compiler omits copy and move constructors entirely, constructing the object directly in the memory location of the target variable. Since C++17, Return Value Optimization (RVO) is mandatory in guaranteed contexts.

slides.title: Return Value Optimization Abbreviation
slides.prompt: Fill in the common acronym for named return value optimization where local named variables are elided during function return.

slides.title: C++17 Guaranteed Copy Elision
slides.prompt: What changed regarding copy elision in the C++17 standard for prvalues?
options: Copy elision became mandatory for prvalues; temporaries are not materialized until necessary, eliminating copy/move overhead completely
Copy elision was deprecated in favor of explicit std::move
Copy elision only applies when compiling with -O3 optimization flag
It applies only to primitive scalar types
slides.correctAnswer: Copy elision became mandatory for prvalues; temporaries are not materialized until necessary, eliminating copy/move overhead completely

slides.title: Copy Elision with Deleted Move Constructor
slides.prompt: Fill in the boolean result in C++17 when returning a non-copyable non-movable prvalue from a function.

slides.title: Preventing NRVO with std::move
slides.prompt: Why is 'return std::move(localObj);' considered an anti-pattern when returning a local variable by value?
options: It inhibits NRVO copy elision, forcing a move operation where zero-copy construction would otherwise occur
It causes compile errors on local objects
It leaks the local stack memory allocation
It converts local variables into static global objects
slides.correctAnswer: It inhibits NRVO copy elision, forcing a move operation where zero-copy construction would otherwise occur

slides.title: Multiple Return Paths Effect on NRVO
slides.prompt: Fill in what happens to NRVO when a function returns different local named variables across conditional branches.

slides.title: Pass-by-Value and Move Paradigm
slides.prompt: In C++11 and later, when should a sink function accept parameters by value (T arg) instead of const T&?
options: When the function needs its own copy anyway, allowing callers to pass rvalues that move seamlessly or lvalues that copy once
Always for all functions regardless of parameter usage
Only when managing primitive types like int or float
Never, pass by value is prohibited in modern C++
slides.correctAnswer: When the function needs its own copy anyway, allowing callers to pass rvalues that move seamlessly or lvalues that copy once

slides.title: Compiler Flag Disabling Copy Elision
slides.prompt: Fill in the GCC/Clang compiler flag used to explicitly turn off copy elision for educational testing.

slides.title: Implicit Move on Local Return
slides.prompt: What occurs if NRVO is not performed when returning a local named variable by value in C++11?
options: The compiler automatically treats the returned local variable as an rvalue, invoking its move constructor if available
The compiler throws a missing move exception
It falls back to deep copy without checking move constructors
The program crashes with stack corruption
slides.correctAnswer: The compiler automatically treats the returned local variable as an rvalue, invoking its move constructor if available
